items.title: feat: speedup `IsEmpty` check
items.body:
## Background

- This command executes in 50ms-300ms on https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/actions
- Codeberg has for every repository its references stored in reftable (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable).
- The forgejo repository has 13019 references.
- All git data is stored on CephFS.

## Changes

From my understanding of git's source-code, `for-each-ref` is able to
iteratively go over refs (and stop after the first reference found).
While `rev-list` is more feature-rich and goes through more hoops than
just 'iterate over refs'.

- Use `git-for-each-ref(1)` to detect if there's any reference.
- Specify a custom format to avoid loading object storage. Mostly a
nice-to-have as it avoids a few `access` syscalls to object storage, we
don't need that information for this function.

## Benchmarks

Codeberg (CephFS):

```
$ hyperfine -N 'git for-each-ref --count=1 --format=found' 'git for-each-ref --count=1' 'git rev-list -n 1 --all'
Benchmark 1: git for-each-ref --count=1 --format=found
  Time (mean ± σ):      12.3 ms ±  10.5 ms    [User: 3.2 ms, System: 3.0 ms]
  Range (min … max):     4.6 ms …  78.0 ms    142 runs

  Warning: Statistical outliers were detected. Consider re-running this benchmark on a quiet system without any interferences from other programs. It might help to use the '--warmup' or '--prepare' options.

Benchmark 2: git for-each-ref --count=1
  Time (mean ± σ):      23.2 ms ±  16.5 ms    [User: 3.6 ms, System: 4.1 ms]
  Range (min … max):     7.9 ms …  87.6 ms    186 runs

Benchmark 3: git rev-list -n 1 --all
  Time (mean ± σ):     199.4 ms ±  75.4 ms    [User: 67.5 ms, System: 25.9 ms]
  Range (min … max):   134.4 ms … 438.2 ms    16 runs

  Warning: Statistical outliers were detected. Consider re-running this benchmark on a quiet system without any interferences from other programs. It might help to use the '--warmup' or '--prepare' options.

Summary
  git for-each-ref --count=1 --format=found ran
    1.89 ± 2.10 times faster than git for-each-ref --count=1
   16.24 ± 15.19 times faster than git rev-list -n 1 --all

```

Locally, same amount of refs (ext4):

```
$ hyperfine -N 'git for-each-ref --count=1 --format=found' 'git for-each-ref --count=1' 'git rev-list -n 1 --all'
Benchmark 1: git for-each-ref --count=1 --format=found (2155 runs)
                mean     ±       σ          min     …     max
  Wall Time      1.1 ms  ±     0.1 ms       1.0 ms  …     1.7 ms
  Memory         6.6 MiB ±     0.1 MiB      6.2 MiB …     7.0 MiB

Benchmark 2: git for-each-ref --count=1 (2713 runs)
                mean     ±       σ          min     …     max
  Wall Time      1.1 ms  ±     0.1 ms       1.0 ms  …     1.8 ms            +4.2%
  Memory         6.8 MiB ±     0.1 MiB      6.3 MiB …     7.1 MiB           +2.5%

Benchmark 3: git rev-list -n 1 --all (591 runs)
                mean     ±       σ          min     …     max
  Wall Time      4.8 ms  ±     0.3 ms       4.3 ms  …     6.6 ms          +339.3%  (4.4x slower)
  Memory         8.7 MiB ±     0.1 MiB      8.2 MiB …     8.9 MiB          +30.9%  (1.3x more)
```

items.title: [v17.0/forgejo] fix: avoid loading unnecessary data during tag creation
items.body:
**Backport:** https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/pulls/14785

I noticed that creating a tag via the web UI of codeberg.org was quite
slow (28-30s).

Tracing showed a interesting SQL query:

```sql
SELECT * FROM `attachment` WHERE `release_id` IN (0) ORDER BY `release_id` ASC, `name` ASC
```

Just before tracing showed that Forgejo was doing a lot of
application (non git/DB) code.

---

- `release_service.CreateNewTag` is called from the web router to handle
creating a new tag, this function prepares a release struct with all the
necessary information (every tag is stored as a release in the
database).
- `createTag` is then called which as first thing calls
`LoadAttributes`.
- `LoadAttributes` assumes the given release was loaded from the
database and thus assumes the ID is non-zero. Loading 148026 attachments
into this release.
